paras: The threatened lynching of Alfred Daniels took place at Trenton, Jones County, North Carolina, on September 14, 1903, when a crowd at the county jail threatened to lynch Daniels, a Black man held for the killing of Farnifold G. Simmons, father of United States Senator F. M. Simmons. No attack was reported; Daniels was moved to New Bern the next morning, and he was later convicted and hanged at Trenton in May 1904. North Carolina papers held up the Senator's appeals as a lesson in restraint, while the Black press noticed the case mainly through an appeal against the exclusion of Black jurors.

F. G. Simmons, an elderly planter, left his home near Pollocksville on Saturday morning, September 12, with his gun to hunt and to stop trespassers, and did not return. His body was found the next day with eighteen No. 4 shot in the breast. Alfred Daniels, described as a "negro" who had worked on the Simmons farm, was arrested and jailed at Trenton.

Feeling ran high in Jones and neighboring Craven County, where "mutters of lynching are often heard," and Sheriff Taylor kept a double guard on the jail. A Trenton dispatch of September 14 described crowds gathering about the Simmons home and talk of lynching, which the Senator personally discouraged. That evening, according to a Raleigh dispatch to the New York Sun, "a large crowd of excited persons" gathered about the jail with threats of lynching, and Senator Simmons asked the men to let the accused have a fair trial.

On the morning of September 15 Sheriff Taylor took Daniels to the Craven County jail at New Bern for safekeeping. The News and Observer's New Bern correspondent wrote that he had been told Daniels would have been lynched had he stayed at Trenton that night, despite the pleas of the Senator and the county's ministers.

The same correspondent reported that the coroner's jury found Simmons was killed by a gun in Daniels's hands, calling an earlier report of a verdict against "parties unknown" erroneous. Daniels was returned to Trenton on November 1, reportedly having told officers that he killed Simmons in self-defense, and was convicted of first-degree murder at the November term of Jones Superior Court. On November 12 Governor Aycock warned Goldsboro, where Daniels was then held, that a mob from Trenton was said to be coming to lynch him; troops were readied, but no one came and the report was called a hoax.

His counsel appealed on the ground that Jones County had discriminated against Black citizens in drawing jurors, but the state Supreme Court found no error and Justice Harlan refused a writ of error. Daniels was hanged privately at Trenton on May 19, 1904, saying he had acted in self-defense and had been "unjustly tried."

Northern papers framed the story around the Senator: the Sun headlined it "SIMMONS APPEALS TO A MOB," while the New-York Tribune's "MAY LYNCH NEGRO MURDERER" stated Daniels's guilt as fact. The News and Observer called the episode "A LESSON IN RESTRAINT," saying the Senator's words "saved the wretch's life," and the Henderson Gold Leaf reprinted a Thomasville editorial against "this crime of lynching criminals." In October the News and Observer reprinted a Washington Post letter by Claude N. Bennett that called the mob's dispersal a "modern miracle" while describing Daniels in racial caricature. Bennett added that had the accused been charged with the offense "usually provocative of lynching," no appeal could have saved him.

No Black-press report of the jail crowd was found. The Savannah Tribune noted only the murder of the Senator's father, and in May 1904 the Indianapolis Freeman twice reported attorney J. C. L. Harris's application to Justice Harlan, stressing that Jones County had no Black names in its jury box.

Accounts of the killing differed: the Sun said Simmons was shot and then clubbed, the News and Observer reported a shotgun wound, the Tribune said he was shot with a pistol and robbed of cotton money, and Bennett described a club. The local News and Observer account is the most detailed. Reports also placed the crowd variously at the jail, at the Simmons home, or around Daniels before he was jailed.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Alfred Daniels
bases: A crowd gathered at the Trenton jail with threats of lynching a Black prisoner accused of murder, and a correspondent was told he would have been lynched had he stayed there (A1, A5, A8); no one was killed, so it is a threatened lynching.

A large crowd threatened to lynch Daniels for the killing of F. G. Simmons, but no attempt on the jail is reported and he was removed to New Bern and later legally hanged (A1, A5, A18); the episode is a threatened lynching, not a lynching.

Independent dispatches from Raleigh, Trenton and New Bern, and the Yorkville Enquirer, agree that crowds gathered and threatened to lynch Daniels and that Senator Simmons urged them to let the law act (A1, A5, A6, A8).

accounts.label: Raleigh wire (New York Sun)
accounts.gist: A large excited crowd gathered at the Trenton jail on the evening of Sept. 14 and threatened lynching; the Senator asked them to allow a fair trial; the sheriff did not expect an attempt.

accounts.label: Trenton and New Bern correspondents (News and Observer)
accounts.gist: Crowds gathered about the Simmons home with talk of lynching, which the Senator discouraged; Daniels was moved to New Bern because he would otherwise have been lynched that night.

accounts.label: Charlotte wire (New-York Tribune) and Yorkville Enquirer
accounts.gist: Daniels killed and robbed Simmons after a cotton sale; a lynching was 'not improbable' and infuriated citizens were dissuaded only by the Senator.

accounts.label: Washington Post letter (Claude N. Bennett)
accounts.gist: An armed mob confronted the captured man and was dispersed by the Senator's appeal before Daniels was taken peaceably to jail.

accounts.label: Daniels's reported statements
accounts.gist: Daniels is reported to have told officers he shot Simmons in self-defense and, on the gallows, that he had been unjustly tried.

accounts.label: Black press
accounts.gist: The Freeman reported his lawyer's appeal that Black men were kept out of the Jones County jury box; the Savannah Tribune noted only the murder of the Senator's father.

framing.detail: The News and Observer's 'A LESSON IN RESTRAINT' and the Gold Leaf's 'A Noble Example' praised the Senator for opposing lynching, while calling Daniels 'the wretch' and the murderer.
Bennett's letter, reprinted as 'SAVED BY SENATOR SIMMONS', called the dispersal a 'modern miracle' while describing Daniels in racial caricature and praising the end of 'negro control'.
Northern wires headlined 'SIMMONS APPEALS TO A MOB' and 'MAY LYNCH NEGRO MURDERER', the latter stating guilt as fact.
The Freeman's 'Race Gleanings' item stressed the race discrimination claim in jury selection without editorial comment.
